case_study_insert.main_stem: Aldervan Engineered Timber (AET) is a cooperative in the engineered timber sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2013 by Jonas and Petra Aldervan, the business presses cross-laminated timber panels and glulam beams from certified Scandinavian spruce for sustainable construction and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. AET plans to invest $1,850,000 in a new CLT press and finger-jointing line, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $1,150,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,640,000 a year, a variable cost of $128 a unit and a selling price of $210, and currently produces 26,500 units a year. AET faces two operational problems: offcut waste is running at 8% of input timber and labour turnover among press operators has reached 13%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Production and Market Report — Q3 2025: The press line laminated 6,800 CLT panels at a reject rate of 2.9%, down from 4.1% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 15 to 7 per month. Market research of 380 architects and contractors found that 62% specify mass timber for low-carbon builds and 55% would pay up to 6% more for certified CLT. Average delivery time is 7 days, and offcut waste is 8% of input timber. A training needs analysis shows 15 of 64 staff have not completed CNC press training; off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $850 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Aldervan Engineered Timber for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.50% to 6.00%, the fifth rise this year, increasing variable-rate borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $11.95 to $12.71 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills. (3) Structural spruce and pine input costs have risen 8.8% year-on-year, while green-building material demand grew 9.3% and overall construction output grew 2.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: AET plans to finance part of its CLT press expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for AET of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs AET nothing in interest or repayment charges, protecting cash flow while the cooperative already carries fixed costs of $1,640,000 a year and has committed to a $700,000 ten-year bank loan for the $1,850,000 press. Avoiding interest on the $1,150,000 retained portion leaves more operating cash to absorb the 8.8% rise in spruce and pine input costs, so AET can defend its $210 selling price and keep the certified CLT programme funded without raising member prices or compromising the 2.9% reject-rate drive.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids collateral and repayment risk, so the $1,150,000 is available without putting the new press at risk of repossession if mass-timber demand disappoints. It also preserves the cooperative's member ownership and democratic control — no external lender can impose covenants over how the press is scheduled, priced or staffed, which matters while green-building demand is growing 9.3% but overall construction output only 2.1%, and while members vote on reinvestment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Aldervan Engineered Timber and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: AET is launching its certified CLT panel range. Consider print advertising in construction trade magazines, social media marketing with sustainability influencers, or sponsoring a televised eco-home series. Which should AET choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Print advertising in construction trade magazines: Specialist magazines would reach the 62% of surveyed architects and contractors specifying mass timber with technical credibility — spans, fire ratings, carbon savings — in a durable format specifiers keep on their desks. However, full-colour space is expensive, monthly circulation slows response, and much of the readership is not decision-ready on a new CLT supplier, making it hard to tie spend to orders against an $1,850,000 investment funded partly by a loan.

Sponsoring a televised eco-home series: A sponsorship slot would give AET the widest possible reach and powerful emotional association with sustainable homes — ideal for the public-facing story of timber replacing concrete and steel. Its drawbacks are very high fees, little control over editorial context, an audience largely irrelevant to professional specifiers, and no targeting of the 55% willing to pay 6% more; broad awareness would not translate into CLT orders.

Social media marketing with sustainability influencers: Working with green-architecture and self-build influencers reaches exactly the 62% specifying mass timber and the 55% paying 6% more for certified CLT, with measurable engagement, low cost per reached specifier and year-round momentum. It demonstrates carbon credentials and real building case studies directly to the 380 architects and contractors in AET's research, though it depends on influencer credibility and consistent quality content.

Recommendation: AET should choose social media marketing with sustainability influencers. It reaches the precise dual-audience of professional specifiers and engaged self-builders identified in research, costs least per qualified lead, runs continuously rather than around one series or monthly issue, and reinforces the certified low-carbon positioning behind the 6% premium. Trade print is rejected as slow and hard to measure; the TV sponsorship is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; influencers plus modest trade-press advertorials later would reinforce professional credibility once first contracts land.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AET with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AET with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade print and TV sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for AET of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its press team, where labour turnover has reached 13%.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives all 64 members a real voice in how the new press and finger-jointing line are set up — shift patterns, quality circles, safety reviews — satisfying their social and esteem needs (Maslow) and aligning the cooperative with its founding principles. Members who design their own work systems are more likely to attend and to challenge the 13% labour turnover, cutting recruitment and onboarding costs for CNC-skilled press operators in a tight labour market.

Point 2: Involving press operators in decisions surfaces practical timber-handling knowledge — how panels twist in humid weeks, where finger-joints fail — driving ideas that reduce the 2.9% reject rate and the 8% offcut waste. Higher involvement raises commitment and keeps 15 untrained staff moving through the $850 CNC courses, protecting the 6,800-panel quarterly output and the credibility AET needs to justify the $1,850,000 investment to members and the bank.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AET's turnover, quality and output.

questions.question_text: AET must improve motivation of its press-team operators. Consider a performance-related bonus linked to panel output or job enrichment through CNC programming responsibilities. Which should AET choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Performance-related bonus linked to panel output: Paying a bonus per panel pressed would directly reward higher throughput towards the 26,500-unit target and give each operator a visible, immediate link between effort and pay — attractive for routine lamination work and easy for the cooperative to administer. Its weaknesses are that it rewards quantity over quality, risking the 2.9% reject rate creeping back up if panels are rushed; it does nothing for the 8% offcut waste; and measured output in single-piece flow can create disputes about what counts as a pressable panel, damaging the cooperative's ethos of equality.

Job enrichment through CNC programming responsibilities: Rotating operators up into programming, tooling offsets and first-off inspection satisfies esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow) and Herzberg's motivators — meaningful, varied, skilled work. It builds the internal bench AET needs for the $1,850,000 line, cuts dependence on two or three CNC experts, and should reduce the 13% turnover among trained staff. Its weaknesses are slower returns, a risk of some operators preferring routine manual roles, and the need for supervision while competence develops.

Decision: AET should choose job enrichment. In a cooperative built on member development, enriching roles attacks the root causes of turnover and the 15-person CNC training gap, and embeds the quality discipline behind certified CLT — attributes a bonus scheme cannot buy. A bonus scheme is rejected as the primary tool because it would likely inflate rejects and waste while doing nothing for skills; AET could add a modest team bonus later tied to quality and waste metrics once reject rates fall below 2.0%, reinforcing both output and pride.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation options with limited application to AET.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both motivation options in the context of AET.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivation options in the context of AET with a well-justified decision covering turnover, quality, skills and cooperative values.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how AET's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,640,000 ÷ ($210 − $128) = $1,640,000 ÷ $82 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $210 − $128 = $82. Answer: contribution per unit is $82.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways AET's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. AET's managers can compare the 20,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 26,500 units, confirming a margin of safety of 6,500 units — enough to tolerate a mild demand dip, but thin enough to justify pushing the certified range hard.
2. Contribution per unit of $82 lets managers model the effect of the 6% certified premium, for example pricing CLT at $222.60, which lifts contribution to $94.60 and lets them judge whether a 6% rise can be passed on to the 55% of buyers willing to pay it.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $1,640,000 and contribution per unit helps managers test whether the $1,850,000 CLT press pays back through incremental units, and set the volume targets needed to service the $700,000 bank loan.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($1,640,000 ÷ 26,500 units + $128 = $189.89 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, pinpoint the offcut waste at 8% of input timber, and decide whether to renegotiate the $128 variable cost with timber suppliers amid the 8.8% input-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $82 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 6,500 units against 26,500-unit output; premium-pricing modelling of the certified range against $1,640,000 fixed costs; affordability testing for the $1,850,000 press against the $700,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $189.89 to tackle 2.9% rejects and 8% offcut waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AET's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has AET's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $6,900,000 revenue − $4,140,000 cost of sales = $2,760,000; 2025 gross profit = $7,800,000 − $4,290,000 = $3,510,000. 2024 operating profit of $828,000 ÷ revenue of $6,900,000 = 12.0%; 2025 operating profit of $1,170,000 ÷ revenue of $7,800,000 = 15.0%. 2024 operating profit of $828,000 ÷ capital employed of $4,600,000 = 18.0%; 2025 operating profit of $1,170,000 ÷ capital employed of $5,200,000 = 22.5%. Revenue grew $900,000 while cost of sales grew only $150,000, lifting gross profit by $750,000.

Evaluation: Profitability has clearly improved. The certified CLT mix added five percentage points to the gross margin to 45.0%, and operating profit grew 41% to $1,170,000, well ahead of revenue growth of about 13%. Capital employed rose $600,000 to fund press upgrades, yet returns on that capital jumped to 22.5%, comfortably covering the $105,000 interest payable. Caution is still required: the 6,500-unit margin of safety is thinner than it looks, spruce and pine input costs rose 8.8%, and the cooperative must keep its 64 members engaged to hold the turnover gains — a slip would push the 2.9% reject rate back up and erode the improved margins.

Conclusion: AET's profitability has improved. Margins and returns on capital employed all rose in 2025, driven by the certified premium, better press efficiency and tighter cost control. To lock in the gains, AET should secure long-term spruce supply contracts, maintain the reject-rate drive below 2.5%, and ensure the new line dilutes the higher capital employed further before contemplating another major investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether AET's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for AET of supplying certified low-carbon CLT instead of conventional concrete or steel frames.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certified low-carbon CLT matches the 62% of 380 surveyed architects and contractors specifying mass timber and the 55% willing to pay up to 6% more, letting AET charge a premium that protects its $82 contribution per unit even as spruce and pine input costs rise 8.8%. It also sequesters carbon in the completed building, helping clients meet their own carbon budgets — a decisive edge in public tenders — and reinforces the cooperative's brand as the green alternative for schools, offices and housing.

Disadvantage: CLT remains exposed to moisture movement, fire-performance regulation and perception risk among insurers and lenders unfamiliar with mass timber. If certification audits slip or a high-profile fire concerns the market, AET could be left with unsellable certified stock and a damaged premium, while the 2.9% reject rate and 8% offcut waste must fall further to keep the $128 variable cost competitive against falling concrete and steel prices.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AET's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.00%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 8.8% rise in structural timber input costs will affect AET. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.50% to 6.00%): On AET's $700,000 ten-year bank loan, a 0.50 percentage point rise adds roughly $3,500 a year — trivial beside fixed costs of $1,640,000. Higher rates could cool clients' construction finance and delay orders, and raise the cost of a later second press, but the direct cash impact is the smallest of the three for AET.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $12.71 per hour): AET employs 64 members, mostly press operators near the minimum wage. The rise adds about $0.76 an hour, roughly $1,580 per worker a year — around $101,000 across the workforce if applied to all 64. That is broadly 9% of 2025 operating profit; in a cooperative that shares surplus with members, wage inflation directly reduces the surplus available and could increase wage pressure in annual dividend debates.

Timber input cost inflation (8.8% spruce and pine): Timber is roughly 70% of the $128 variable cost (about $90). An 8.8% rise adds about $7.90 per unit; at 26,500 units that is roughly $210,000 a year — nearly a fifth of operating profit — before price recovery. AET can recover part through the 6% certified premium and annual price reviews, but not all, and the 6,500-unit margin of safety leaves little room to absorb the remainder.

Conclusion: The 8.8% rise in structural timber input costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every one of the 26,500 units sold and totals roughly $210,000 a year — about double the wage increase and sixty times the loan interest rise — directly compressing the $82 contribution and the certified premium AET depends on. AET must lock in multi-year spruce contracts, accelerate waste reduction below 6%, and index prices to timber indices; the wage rise is a serious second threat and the rate rise the least damaging, though all three demand tighter margin management through 2027.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to AET.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AET's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AET with a well-justified judgement that timber input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
